newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: PCS sees petrochemical prices falling.
newsitem.headline: PCS sees petrochemical prices falling.

text.p: The opening of a major plant in Singapore and new ones in India, Kuwait and Thailand are expected to keep petrochemical prices under pressure for the next two to three years, the head of the Petrochemical Corporation of Singapore (PCS) said on Tuesday.
"Prices will come under pressure in the next two to three years," managing director Takayuki Okada told Reuters in an interview.

"Competition will get tougher as new capacities come on stream over the next few years. A number of the new producers will probably have to export the balance of their products as their domestic markets cannot fully absorb the new capacities."

Okada said the drop was not expected to be of the magnitude seen in 1993 and 1994 when prices fell around 30 percent after new plants opened in South Korea and Southeast Asia. He declined to make a firm prediction on how far they would fall.
In the second quarter of 1997, PCS will open its 515,000 tonne per year ethylene plant that is at the heart of a US$2.4 billion expansion.
India's Reliance Industries started up a 700,000 tonne-per-year plant this month that will operate at full capacity by the end of March.

Due to open by the end of 1997 is a US$2 billion complex in Kuwait that will produce 450,000 tonnes of ethylene a year. In early 1998, Taiwan's Formosa Petrochemical Corporation plans to open a new plant of similar size.
Thai Petrochemical Industry Plc is building a 700,000 tonne-per-year plant that is expected to be ready by the end of 1998.
These planned expansions also include the building of plants to produce derivative products such as polyethylene and polypropylene, used to make plastic products.
Okada said he was confident that PCS would be able to weather the coming storm as it did during the industry's cyclical bust years, with 1993 and 1994 being the most recent.
"We had a very good year in 1995 but 1996 was not so good," he said, adding that 1997 was going to be a difficult year.

"Our project is not a greenfield development -- the infrastructure from Complex 1 is already there," he said. "We are confident we will be competitive and we are optimistic about the success of our PCS II project."
PCS operates a 450,000 tonne-per-year ethylene plant at Pulau Ayer Merbau, one of a group of small islands off the southern coast of Singapore.
The company is a 50-50 joint venture between Royal Dutch Shell and a consortium of Japanese companies.

The startup of the new ethylene plants has led to a squeeze in the supply of naptha feedstock, with prices now at a new post-Gulf War high of about $235 per tonne cost-and-freight Japan -- the benchmark price for the Asian market.
To ensure a steady supply of naphtha, PCS has secured term contracts for up to 80 percent of its needs, Okada said.
"In anticipation of next year's feedstock requirement, we have already increased the intake quantities in the term contracts this year," he added.
